titre: The Odessa Steps massacre never took place on those steps
accroche: The most famous scene in Battleship Potemkin is so convincing that people take it for documentary. No source places this massacre at that spot.
contenu_vulgarise:
Soldiers in white tunics march down an endless staircase, in step, firing on a crowd that refuses to back away. A woman collapses, hit. Her baby's carriage tips over and rolls down the steps, alone, among the bodies. The Odessa Steps sequence in *Battleship Potemkin* has been reprised in dozens of films, up to the central station shootout in Brian De Palma's *The Untouchables*. Many viewers know it before they have even seen the original film. In collective memory, it has become a massacre that really did take place on those steps, one day in 1905.

## A massacre that didn't happen there

The film commemorates the twentieth anniversary of the mutiny on the battleship Potemkin, in June 1905: sailors, exasperated by the rotten food they are served, rise up against their officers. The ship then calls at Odessa, where its arrival sets off riots in other parts of the city. The Times of London and the British consul on the scene report that tsarist troops did fire on those rioters, elsewhere in the city, killing hundreds. But no source places a daytime shooting on the port's great staircase, as it is filmed. The scene, however precise in its details, the student in uniform, the old woman with the pince-nez, is an invention of Sergei Eisenstein, who concentrates in a single place and instant a violence that was really exercised, but scattered elsewhere in the city.

## What this changes

The critic Roger Ebert put it bluntly: that there was, in reality, no tsarist massacre on the Odessa Steps does nothing to diminish the scene's power, and the irony is that Eisenstein filmed it so well that this massacre is now evoked as if it had really taken place at that precise spot. It is the very principle of Soviet montage, of which Eisenstein was one of the theorists: the meaning of a scene comes not from the shots taken separately but from their collision, like two forces that, in clashing, produce a reality greater than either. Applied to History itself, this principle produces a massacre truer than the facts that inspired it, to the point of replacing them in the public's memory. What follows confirms it in another way: Stalin himself would have the film banned in the Soviet Union, fearing that a crowd inspired by the Potemkin's sailors might turn against his own power. The fiction Eisenstein had put at the service of one regime ended up frightening the next.

citation.texte: That there was, in fact, no czarist massacre on the Odessa Steps scarcely diminishes the power of the scene. The czar’s troops shot innocent civilians elsewhere in Odessa, and Eisenstein, in concentrating those killings and finding the perfect setting for them, was doing his job as a director. It is ironic that he did it so well that today, the bloodshed on the Odessa Steps is often referred to as if it really happened.

carte.punch: No source places the massacre, as filmed, on the Odessa staircase.
carte.idee: In Battleship Potemkin, soldiers massacre the crowd on the Odessa staircase. No source places a daytime shooting at that spot: troops fired elsewhere in the city, killing hundreds. Eisenstein concentrated that violence into one scene, truer than the facts.

quiz.question: Why do historians call the massacre scene on the Odessa Steps in Battleship Potemkin an invention?
choix: Because no source places a daytime shooting on that particular staircase, even though troops did fire on rioters elsewhere in the city
Because the scene was never shot in Odessa, but in a reconstructed studio in Moscow
Because the mutiny on the battleship Potemkin itself never happened, contrary to what the film tells
Because Eisenstein himself supposedly admitted, years later, to having invented the sequence entirely for reasons of censorship
quiz.explication: The Times of London and the British consul do report firing by tsarist troops on rioters in Odessa, with hundreds dead, but no source places a daytime shooting on this great staircase, as it is filmed: Eisenstein concentrates in one place and instant a violence that was really exercised, but scattered elsewhere in the city.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which real event does the film commemorate, twenty years after the fact?
choix: The mutiny of the sailors of the battleship Potemkin, who rose up against their officers in June 1905
The October Revolution of 1917, which overthrows the Russian provisional government
The siege of Sevastopol during the Crimean War
The general strike of the Odessa port dockworkers in 1903
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The film commemorates the twentieth anniversary of the June 1905 mutiny, when sailors exasperated by rotten food rose up against their officers, an event distinct from the 1917 revolution or the siege of Sevastopol.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which cinematic principle, of which Eisenstein is one of the theorists, explains his method in this scene?
choix: The long take, which refuses any cut to preserve the unity of real time
Soviet montage, in which meaning is born from the collision of shots rather than from each one taken separately
Cross-cutting, which switches between two simultaneous places to create suspense
The point-of-view camera, which puts the viewer in a character's exact place
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Soviet montage holds that the meaning of a scene is the product of the collision of shots, like two forces that, in clashing, produce a reality greater than either one taken alone.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why does Stalin have the film banned in the Soviet Union, later on?
choix: Because the film was judged too expensive to produce for its time
Because Eisenstein had left the country without authorization before the film's release
Because religious authorities had protested against the violent scenes
Because he fears that a crowd, inspired by the rebellious sailors, will turn against his power
quiz_supplementaire.explication: This card says so explicitly: Stalin fears that a crowd inspired by the example of the rebellious sailors will in turn rise against the power he himself wields.
